query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Isothermal aging treatments can be used to control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys by tuning the chemical ordering and precipitation behavior, thereby influencing mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy (eutectic or dual-phase microstructure with FCC and B2 phases) before any targeted aging treatment.
generation.intervention: Application of controlled isothermal aging treatments at selected temperatures (e.g., around 600°C versus 750°C) for a fixed duration followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Aging under inert atmosphere at specific temperatures (e.g., 600°C or 750°C) for approximately 20 hours, with a controlled heating rate prior to aging and water quenching afterward.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of ordered precipitates (such as L1₂ domains) and changes in the morphology and coherency of phase boundaries between the constituent phases.
generation.mechanism: The isothermal aging promotes chemical ordering and controlled precipitation. At lower aging temperatures (e.g., 600°C), highly ordered and fine precipitates form, which may lead to embrittlement due to jagged, incoherent phase boundaries. At higher aging temperatures (e.g., 750°C), the precipitates grow slightly larger and become off-stoichiometric, leading to improved phase boundary coherence and enabling deformation through multiple slip systems.
generation.predicted_outcome: Depending on the precise aging conditions chosen, the alloy will exhibit either embrittlement (if aging yields highly ordered fine precipitates) or recover ductility along with enhanced strength (if aging promotes a beneficial size and ordering of precipitates), resulting in a tuning of mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or homogenized alloy microstructure lacking controlled precipitate formation through aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The optimal aging parameters are composition-dependent and sensitive to small changes in temperature and time; the mechanism may differ if the starting microstructure deviates significantly from the eutectic or dual-phase state.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature and time window for optimal phase evolution remains uncertain and might vary with small compositional shifts and processing history in the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate several AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy samples by vacuum induction melting. Subject different sample sets to aging at 600°C, 750°C, and, as a control, no aging (as-cast). Rapidly quench after aging. Characterize the evolved microstructure using TEM and atom probe tomography to detect precipitate size, ordering, and phase boundary coherence. Conduct mechanical tensile tests to evaluate changes in yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility.
measurements: TEM imaging for precipitate morphology and size
APT for chemical ordering and stoichiometry of precipitates
EBSD for phase identification and boundary coherence
Mechanical tensile tests for ductility and strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the controlled aging treatments do not produce significant changes in precipitate characteristics (size, order, coherence) or do not result in measurable differences in mechanical properties compared to as-cast samples, then the hypothesis that isothermal aging controls phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs is falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) containing face-centered cubic (FCC) and ordered body-centered cubic (B2) phases. Processing: Vacuum induction levitation melting followed by isothermal aging at 520, 600, 700, 750, 800, 1000, and 1200 °C for 20 hours at a heating rate of 300 °C/h and rapid quenching in water.
